# 5.3 Production costs and revenue

## Notes

### B-6145-5.3-001 Set a period, output and cost boundary
Costs describe resources used in production, while revenue describes receipts from sales. Begin with a specified period and a consistent output unit. A weekly total cannot be divided by annual output to obtain a meaningful weekly unit cost. Likewise, a cost stated only for materials is not the full cost of production. The terms total and average indicate different measures; fixed and variable classify costs by their response to output in the relevant period.

Use an invented weekly example at Red Valley Soap Works. Existing capacity can produce up to 300 comparable bars. Weekly fixed cost is N$600. Variable cost is N$4 per bar over the supplied range. At 100 bars, total variable cost is N$400 and total cost N$1,000. At 200 bars, total variable cost is N$800 and total cost N$1,400. These values use the same capacity and period. Their increase does not mean every category of cost has increased.

The key formulas are total cost = fixed cost + variable cost, and average cost = total cost / output. The first combines cost categories; the second converts a total into a per-unit measure. At 100 bars average cost is N$10 per bar; at 200 it is N$7. Total cost rises by N$400 while average cost falls by N$3 per bar. Those statements are compatible because the total is spread over twice as much output. Keep the units visible when comparing them.

To organise the schedule, record each output alongside fixed cost, total variable cost and total cost. Then divide each total by that row’s output when a unit measure is needed. Check the addition before division: if fixed and variable costs do not sum to total cost, a later correct division still produces the wrong economic result. At positive output, average fixed and average variable cost should likewise sum to average total cost.

### B-6145-5.3-002 Total cost includes both categories
Total cost is the full cost of producing a specified output in a period. It adds total fixed and total variable costs rather than selecting whichever one seems most relevant to a decision. A soap producer using rented premises and materials incurs both. If the premises charge remains due even with no production, it remains part of the weekly total cost under the stated arrangement.

At 100 bars, the invented N$600 fixed cost plus N$400 variable cost gives total cost N$1,000. At zero bars, variable cost is zero in this particular schedule, but fixed cost remains N$600, so total cost is N$600. The absence of production does not make every payment disappear. Do not assume that a zero-output firm has no costs or that a cost stops being fixed because it is inconvenient.

Total cost should be compared with total revenue when finding total profit. Subtracting average cost from total revenue mixes money per bar with money per week. If the case gives a unit cost, multiply it by the relevant output before using it as a total, ensuring that the figure really covers all relevant costs. A partial materials total alone cannot establish profit. Similarly, the word total needs a defined boundary: a daily total of materials is still not a weekly total of all production costs.

### B-6145-5.3-003 Average cost measures each output unit’s share
Average cost is total cost per unit of output. Divide the full cost for the period by the number of comparable units produced in that period. At 200 soap bars, N$1,400 divided by 200 gives N$7 per bar. This is a calculated average; it does not mean that each physical bar required a separate N$7 payment or that the next bar will add exactly N$7 to cost.

Average cost can also be separated into average fixed and average variable cost. With weekly fixed cost N$600 at 200 bars, average fixed cost is N$3. Variable cost N$800 divided by 200 gives N$4. The sum is N$7. This breakdown explains the fall from N$10 at 100 bars: the fixed component falls from N$6 to N$3, while the supplied variable cost per bar remains N$4.

At zero output, average cost is undefined because division by zero is not possible. Report the known total cost without assigning a zero average cost. The period and output measure still matter at positive output: different bar sizes or quality grades may not be directly comparable. A low measured cost per bar is not necessarily evidence of better performance if the bars have become smaller or defective. Use the comparable units stated in the example.

### B-6145-5.3-004 Fixed means independent of current output within a range
A fixed cost does not change as output varies over the relevant short-run range and period. An agreed premises charge of N$600 a week can remain due whether the workshop makes 0, 100 or 200 bars. The classification applies to the stated arrangement rather than fixing the payment for all future periods. A new rental agreement, larger premises or a different period can change the amount; those changes lie outside the unchanged arrangement being analysed.

Distinguish total fixed cost from fixed cost per unit. N$600 spread across 100 bars contributes N$6 to each bar’s average cost. Spread across 200 bars, it contributes N$3. The fixed total remains N$600. Saying that fixed cost falls as output expands is ambiguous unless the statement specifies the per-unit component. Within existing capacity, falling average fixed cost can help reduce average total cost, but a rise in another component may offset it.

Capacity matters. If producing 400 bars requires renting an additional room, the previous fixed-cost assumption cannot simply be carried beyond 300-bar capacity. Use the new stated cost when comparing that option. In the long run a firm can change its scale and inputs more extensively; topic 5.4 owns the resulting economies and diseconomies of scale. Spreading an existing weekly premises cost across more bars is the narrower short-run mechanism in this example.

### B-6145-5.3-005 Variable cost and unit rates
A variable cost changes with output. Materials used for additional soap bars are a straightforward example. In the invented simple schedule, variable cost is N$4 per bar, so 100 bars use N$400 and 200 use N$800. The constant unit amount is an assumption of this schedule, not part of the definition of a variable cost.

In another case, extra output might require overtime at a higher rate or lead to more waste. Variable cost would then rise more rapidly at high output. Alternatively, more efficient use of materials could reduce the variable amount per unit over a range. Read the supplied conditions before multiplying all output by one rate. A rising total variable cost does not establish that its average rises: if output grows in the same proportion, average variable cost is unchanged.

Cost categories depend on the payment arrangement and period. A guaranteed weekly salary can be fixed over a stated short-run range, while piece-rate payments may vary directly with units made. Electricity may include a standing charge and a usage charge, giving fixed and variable components. Classify the supplied payment component using its stated terms. This is why a useful example states how the payment responds to output.

### B-6145-5.3-006 Revenue uses sales rather than unsold production
Total revenue is sales receipts over a period. Average revenue is revenue per unit sold, calculated as total revenue divided by sales quantity. Production and sales need not be equal: unsold goods may remain in stock. Where a workshop makes 120 bars but sells 100 for N$8 each, total revenue is N$800 and average revenue N$8 per bar sold. Dividing by 120 would answer a different ratio and would not give average revenue per unit sold.

Average revenue also differs from marginal revenue. Marginal revenue measures the additional revenue from selling an extra unit. Suppose total revenue at 100 units sold is N$800 and at 101 units is N$806. Marginal revenue for that extra unit is N$6. Average revenue at 101 is N$806 divided by 101, approximately N$7.98 per unit sold. The difference between totals is not the same operation as dividing one total by quantity.

When every unit sells at an unchanged uniform price, average and marginal revenue can coincide with that price. This special case does not make the definitions equivalent. A change in the price needed to sell more can make additional revenue different from the average. Keep marginal revenue limited to this distinction and the profit-maximisation reasoning in topic 5.1. Revenue is also distinct from profit: costs must be subtracted before the sales receipts can be interpreted as an excess available to the firm.

### B-6145-5.3-007 Total revenue: money from sales
Total revenue is the money received from selling output in a period. At one uniform price, multiply that price by units sold. Selling 200 bars at N$8 gives N$1,600. If only 150 of the produced bars sell, revenue at that price is N$1,200. The remaining production has not generated sales receipts in this example merely because resources were used to make it.

With different selling prices, add the revenue from each group. An invented sale of 100 bars at N$8 and 50 at N$6 gives N$800 plus N$300, or N$1,100. Multiplying all 150 by the higher price would overstate receipts. State sales volumes and prices clearly before applying a shortcut formula.

A larger sales quantity does not establish a larger total revenue when the price also changes. Compare 100 units at N$10, giving N$1,000, with 150 at N$6, giving N$900. More units are sold but receipts fall. Topic 3.3 explains the price-elasticity link to revenue. The immediate requirement here is to use both the sales quantity and price information instead of treating output growth as an automatic increase in receipts.

### B-6145-5.3-008 Average revenue: receipts per unit sold
Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity sold. At a uniform N$8 selling price, N$1,600 from 200 bars gives N$8 per bar. This equals the price because each sale contributes that same amount. The equality is conditional on uniform pricing; the definition remains total sales revenue per unit sold.

For the mixed-price example, N$1,100 from 150 bars gives average revenue of approximately N$7.33 per bar sold. It lies between N$6 and N$8 because the units are split between those prices. A simple unweighted mean of the two prices, N$7, would be incorrect because twice as many units sell at N$8 as at N$6. Sales-weighted averaging follows directly from dividing the combined receipts by the combined sales quantity.

Average revenue cannot be calculated at zero sales by dividing zero by zero. Report that no average-revenue value is established. Nor should average revenue be called average profit: if average cost is N$7 and average revenue N$8 for the same quantity produced and sold, the N$1 difference is unit profit under that matched condition. N$8 itself still describes receipts before cost. Keeping the measures distinct prevents an apparent price advantage being confused with the final profitability of production.

For 200 bars both produced and sold, that N$1 unit profit corresponds to N$200 total profit. Multiplying the matched unit difference by 200 gives the same answer as subtracting N$1,400 total cost from N$1,600 total revenue. This provides a consistency check under the stated equal production-and-sales condition. If inventories change, do not silently use different production and sales quantities in a unit shortcut. Follow the particular costs and revenue recognised in the supplied period, and explain the boundary where needed instead of assuming all production earns receipts immediately.

### B-6145-5.3-009 Changing output can move totals and averages differently
Within existing capacity, producing more generally requires more variable inputs. Total cost can rise while average cost falls because the fixed component is spread over more units. In the invented schedule, increasing from 100 to 200 bars raises total cost N$1,000 to N$1,400 but lowers average cost N$10 to N$7. The fixed-cost spreading condition explains the direction; it is not a promise that average cost falls at every output.

Beyond some point, adding more of a variable factor to fixed equipment can produce progressively smaller additions to output. This is diminishing returns. Crowding workers around a fixed-size mixer may reduce each extra worker’s contribution. More input may then be needed for each extra bar, tending to raise additional production cost. This short-run condition differs from changing the scale of all inputs over the long run. Do not label every rise in unit cost a diseconomy of scale.

Revenue depends on sales. If all bars sell at N$8, total revenue at 100 and 200 bars is N$800 and N$1,600. Comparing with the schedule’s total costs gives a loss of N$200 at 100 and profit N$200 at 200. The higher output helps under these particular demand and cost conditions. If the extra bars cannot be sold, production may add cost without the expected receipts. If a price cut is required, recalculate revenue rather than retaining the original price for every unit.

Profit is total revenue minus total cost. A revenue increase can coincide with a profit fall if costs rise more. Conversely, falling receipts can coexist with higher profit if relevant costs fall sufficiently. Work with matched totals for the same period and state the sales assumption. These calculations concern a firm’s operations; topic 7.3 covers the different meaning and measurement of national output.

### B-6145-5.3-010 Technology changes the cost structure
Technology can change capacity, quality and the factor combination. New equipment may increase fixed commitments while reducing material waste or labour time per unit. Whether total cost falls then depends on output. A lower variable cost is not sufficient evidence that the technology is cheaper overall.

Compare invented same-quality weekly methods. The existing method has N$600 fixed cost and N$4 variable cost per bar. A new method has N$1,000 fixed cost and N$2 variable cost per bar; these figures include all relevant costs for the comparison. At 100 bars, existing total cost is N$1,000 and new total cost N$1,200. The N$200 variable saving is smaller than the N$400 added fixed commitment. At 300 bars, existing total cost is N$1,800 and new total cost N$1,600. The N$600 variable saving now exceeds that N$400 commitment.

If all 300 bars sell at the same N$8 price, revenue under either method is N$2,400. Profit is N$600 with the existing method and N$800 with the new one. At 100 bars sold at N$8, both lose money, with losses N$200 and N$400 respectively. New technology is preferable at the stated high output for profit comparison, but less attractive at low output. Sales and feasibility still matter: a cheaper cost at an unsaleable output does not justify producing it.

Training, reliability and maintenance affect whether these costs and quality can be achieved. Technology may also improve product quality and demand, but a numerical revenue gain needs evidence rather than assumption. Evaluate the changed cost structure alongside the output that can realistically be sold. This preserves the distinction between a potential technical improvement and a demonstrated economic advantage.

At 200 bars the two methods each cost N$1,400: the N$400 variable saving exactly matches the added fixed commitment. This equality identifies the cost-comparison boundary in this particular schedule. It is not a claim of zero profit, since that depends separately on revenue. At the stated N$8 price, each method earns N$200 profit there.

1	# 5.4 Economies and diseconomies of scale
2	
3	## Notes
4	
5	### B-6145-5.4-001 Classify the relationship before naming integration
6	Integration brings business activities under common ownership or control. It can occur when firms combine or one acquires another. To classify it, identify the original firm’s industry and production stage, then compare the acquired activity. Buying from a supplier under an ordinary contract is not by itself integration: the ownership or control relationship must change. Growth within an existing business is also distinct from combining previously separate firms.
7	
8	Use an invented chain in Namibia: clay extraction supplies a tile manufacturer, which supplies a tile retailer serving households. The manufacturer is the reference point. Combining with another tile manufacturer is horizontal integration. Acquiring the retailer is forward vertical integration, moving towards the customer. Acquiring the clay supplier is backward vertical integration, moving towards the source of inputs. The direction follows the chain, not whether the acquired business is geographically north, nearer or larger.
9	
10	Integration can change capacity, access to supplies or distribution, but the label does not prove success. Costs of acquisition, coordination and operation still matter. A larger combined firm may gain economies of scale while facing new management difficulties. Keep the classification question separate from the evaluation of cost consequences. A clear explanation first establishes the relationship and then examines the supplied benefits and limitations.
11	
12	### B-6145-5.4-002 Horizontal: the same industry and stage
13	Horizontal integration combines firms at the same production stage in the same industry. If the invented Dune Tile Works acquires another tile manufacturer, both turn inputs into tiles at the manufacturing stage. Common ownership can combine production capacity, customers or distribution arrangements. Acquiring a supplier or retailer would be vertical rather than horizontal because the stage differs.
14	
15	Potential cost gains could come from using a larger specialist machine, consolidating duplicated administration or negotiating purchases for a greater volume. These are possible consequences requiring evidence; they are not contained in the definition. Two factories operating separately under one owner may retain much of their previous cost structure. Integrating their records and processes can itself require resources.
16	
17	To identify the type, ask whether the activities would have competed at the same stage before combination. Two tile manufacturers fit; a tile manufacturer and a tile shop do not, even though both concern tiles. Using the product alone as the test misses the stage distinction. A statement that a firm simply becomes larger is also insufficient to distinguish horizontal integration from expansion through new premises or vertical integration.
18	
19	### B-6145-5.4-003 Forward: towards customers
20	Forward vertical integration combines an original firm with a later stage towards the final customer. When Dune Tile Works acquires its tile retailer, manufacturing is linked to retail distribution under common control. The manufacturer moves downstream in the production chain. It has not acquired another manufacturer, so the combination is not horizontal.
21	
22	Direct control of retailing can improve access to customers or information about preferences. It may let the firm coordinate delivery and presentation more closely. However, it also requires retail skills, premises and stock management. A manufacturer’s technical experience does not automatically establish competence in selling to households. The likely benefit should be weighed against the resources needed to perform that later activity.
23	
24	The reference point matters. Describe the original firm and the acquired stage rather than saying that ownership simply moves forward. Manufacturing followed by retailing is a sequence of activities, not a sequence determined by the date the businesses were founded. A manufacturer supplying an independent retailer remains a trading relationship unless the case states the relevant ownership or control change. This boundary makes the classification economically meaningful.
25	
26	### B-6145-5.4-004 Backward: towards the inputs
27	Backward vertical integration combines an original firm with an earlier stage supplying its inputs. If Dune Tile Works acquires a clay extraction business, it extends ownership towards raw materials. The original manufacturer is still the reference point. The fact that clay eventually becomes a tile does not make its supplier the same manufacturing stage.
28	
29	Control of a supplier may help coordinate deliveries or the required input quality. It can reduce dependence on an independent supplier if the acquired operation is reliable. Yet ownership does not remove extraction costs, geological limits or management problems. A previously competitive independent supply arrangement may even be cheaper than operating the supplier directly. Evaluate full costs rather than treating an internal transfer as a free input.
30	
31	Compare the directions explicitly: retailer acquisition is forward from manufacturing, while input-supplier acquisition is backward. A useful classification states the activity acquired and its position in the chain. This prevents the common mistake of judging direction by the destination of money: a manufacturer pays its supplier, but the payment flow does not turn input acquisition into forward integration. The production sequence determines the label.
32	
33	### B-6145-5.4-005 Economies of scale lower long-run average cost
34	Economies of scale are reductions in long-run average cost as production scale increases. In the long run the firm can adjust its scale and inputs rather than merely add workers to unchanged equipment. The cost benefit concerns the average per unit. Total cost can rise because much more is produced even while the unit cost falls. A bigger business is not evidence of an economy unless the relevant cost-per-unit mechanism is established.
35	
36	Technical economies can arise when a larger operation makes efficient specialised equipment worthwhile. A small tile business may be unable to use a large kiln effectively; sustained larger output can make the technology economical. Managerial economies can arise when specialist purchasing or production managers improve decisions over an operation large enough to justify their employment. Both depend on the productive benefit exceeding the associated costs.
37	
38	Purchasing economies may allow bulk discounts when suppliers’ savings or bargaining conditions support a lower input price. Financial economies can arise if a larger, well-established firm obtains more favourable finance under the stated risk conditions; lenders are not obliged to offer it cheaper credit merely because it is large. Marketing economies can spread an effective campaign’s cost over a larger sales volume. These are distinct routes to lower unit costs, not reasons to count the same saving repeatedly.
39	
40	Internal economies come from growth of the individual firm. External economies come from growth of the industry outside that firm. A cluster of tile producers could attract specialist repair providers or training, improving access for participating firms. An individual firm can benefit without itself expanding. Identify whose growth causes the advantage before using internal or external.
41	
42	For an original numerical illustration, imagine long-run output options of 100, 200 and 300 comparable units with average costs N$12, N$9 and N$8. These options permit adjustment of all inputs; they are not a fixed-kiln short-run schedule. To plot them, put output on the horizontal axis and long-run average cost in N$ per unit on the vertical axis. Mark the three labelled points. Their falling pattern illustrates economies over that range, while an explanation must still name the relevant technical, purchasing or other mechanism. The points alone do not prove which cause operates.
43	
44	The distinction between firm and industry growth can be tested with a repair service. If Dune Tile Works expands enough to employ its own specialist kiln engineer efficiently, that is a potential internal managerial or technical advantage from its own scale. If several independent tile producers attract a nearby specialist repair business that serves them all, the improved access can be an external economy. In the second case, Dune Tile Works may benefit while its own output remains unchanged. The same useful service can therefore enter different explanations depending on the source of the advantage.
45	
46	Risk sharing can also support a larger operation where it sells several products or reaches several markets. A fall in one source of sales may then have a smaller effect on total activity. This does not eliminate risk or directly demonstrate a unit-cost reduction; diversification adds coordination and may involve related demand changes. Explain the relevant saving or stability mechanism if a case relies on it rather than treating a longer product list as sufficient proof of economies.
47	
48	### B-6145-5.4-006 Diseconomies of scale raise long-run average cost
49	Diseconomies of scale are increases in long-run average cost as production scale increases. An expanding organisation can become harder to coordinate. Messages passing through additional management layers may be delayed or distorted, leading to mismatched orders and waste. Departments may duplicate work or act on inconsistent information. If these problems add cost faster than they add useful output, unit cost rises.
50	
51	Motivation can also weaken if workers feel remote from decisions or responsibility becomes unclear. Supervision and communication may then require more resources, with rework reducing usable output. These outcomes are possible organisational effects, not proof that large firms must be badly managed. Effective delegation and clear information can limit them. The task is to explain the supplied difficulty rather than make size itself an automatic cause.
52	
53	External diseconomies arise when industry growth creates disadvantages outside one firm. For example, congestion on a shared access route can delay several producers, or competition for a scarce local input can raise its price. Distinguish these industry effects from a firm's internal communication problem. A single firm can experience external pressure even if its own scale is unchanged.
54	
55	Extend the invented long-run illustration: output 300, 400 and 500 units has average cost N$8, N$9 and N$11. Plot output horizontally and long-run average cost vertically, marking the three points. The rising section illustrates diseconomies over that range. Combined with the earlier falling points, the schedule has its lowest listed average cost at 300. It does not establish an exact minimum between unlisted points.
56	
57	Do not confuse this with diminishing returns. Diminishing returns concern adding a variable factor while another remains fixed, as when more workers share one unchanged kiln. Diseconomies concern larger long-run scale, where inputs can be adjusted. Both can be associated with rising costs, but the conditions and mechanisms differ. A classification must use those conditions rather than the upward direction of a cost figure alone.
58	
59	### B-6145-5.4-007 Compare the net unit-cost effect
60	Expansion can create economies and diseconomies together. A larger order may secure cheaper materials while a more complex delivery system adds coordination costs. The net effect on long-run average cost depends on their relative size. Naming an economy does not prove the combined average cost falls; naming a management problem does not prove the whole expansion raises it.
61	
62	Use invented per-unit changes with comparable output quality. Technical and purchasing gains save N$3 per unit, while additional coordination adds N$1. Net average cost falls N$2. In a more complex expansion, the same N$3 saving might be outweighed by N$4 added coordination cost, raising the average N$1. These calculations illustrate the balance rather than assigning a guaranteed cost pattern to a particular size.
63	
64	Lower average cost can support profit at a given selling price when output is sold, but it is not sufficient to establish a profit increase in isolation. Prices, sales and total commitments also matter. Likewise, lower average cost does not mean the total resource bill falls. At 100 units with average cost N$12, total cost is N$1,200; at 300 with average cost N$8 it is N$2,400. The firm spends more in total while producing much more efficiently per unit.
65	
66	A conclusion should therefore state the objective, the relevant scale range, the net cost effect and the sales condition. An expansion beyond the lowest listed unit-cost option might still have other attractions, but it cannot be justified as a unit-cost saving from this schedule. Keep the evidence and the proposed goal aligned.
67	
68	Integration and economies of scale should not be used as synonyms. An acquisition changes ownership relationships; an economy of scale changes long-run average cost as scale increases. Integration may enable a saving, but it can also leave production arrangements largely unchanged or introduce costly duplication. A manufacturer acquiring its retailer gains a later-stage activity, not an automatic reduction in manufacturing cost. Trace how the combination affects resources and usable output before claiming the unit-cost benefit.
69	
70	Where the data show lower average cost, test whether the compared products and quality are consistent. Producing smaller or less durable tiles can make a unit figure fall without an equivalent gain in satisfying customer requirements. The scale schedules here explicitly use comparable units so that the cost comparison concerns scale rather than a changed product. This condition belongs in any extension of the numerical argument.
71	
72	### B-6145-5.4-008 Why firms differ in size
73	Firm size is influenced by the market it can serve, the capital it can secure and the organisation it can manage. Measures of size also differ: workers employed, sales, output and assets need not rank firms identically. A capital-intensive producer may have valuable equipment but relatively few workers. Use the stated measure rather than assuming size always means employment.
74	
75	Small firms can remain viable through personal service, specialised products or flexibility. A customised tile restorer may serve a narrow local demand better with close customer contact than a large standardised operation would. Limited economies of scale can reduce the pressure to expand. The owner may also value control or lack the funds and organisation for growth.
76	
77	These explanations interact. Capital can provide capacity without creating customers; a large market can offer opportunity without supplying finance; management can coordinate resources without guaranteeing sales. Compare the actual constraints in the case. A firm’s small current size is not by itself proof of inefficiency, just as a large current size is not proof that expansion has been successful.
78	
79	### B-6145-5.4-009 Market size limits saleable output
80	A large sustained market can support sales needed to use larger-scale production efficiently. If confirmed customers want standard tiles in high volumes, equipment and specialist staff may be used sufficiently to justify expansion. Demand must be saleable at relevant prices, not merely a statement that people like the product. Willingness and ability to buy matter.
81	
82	A narrow market may leave large equipment underused. An invented village producer of customised memorial tiles might have only a few orders each month. Building a large standard production plant would not create enough buyers by itself. Exporting or finding new markets could change the demand constraint, but those opportunities require evidence and may add transport or marketing costs.
83	
84	Market stability matters as well as its current size. A temporary festival order might not support permanent capacity whose costs continue after the event. A stable stream of orders provides stronger support for sustained scale. When recommending growth, state why demand is expected to last and what would happen if sales weaken. This connects market size to feasible utilisation rather than treating expansion as an end in itself.
85	
86	### B-6145-5.4-010 Capital available limits feasible expansion
87	Growth may need premises, machinery and funds for materials before customers pay. The economic resource capital includes produced means of production; finance enables the firm to acquire and operate them. A profitable-looking proposal can remain infeasible if the firm cannot secure the required funds on terms it can meet. Cash availability and expected profitability are related but different questions.
88	
89	Suppose expansion requires an invented N$200,000 initial outlay while the owner can provide N$60,000 and no additional funding is currently available. The N$140,000 gap constrains that proposal even if a large market exists. A smaller staged expansion might fit the resources, while an outside investor or lender could change the position if willing to supply funds. Their willingness is not established merely by the owner wanting to grow.
90	
91	Borrowing can create a repayment commitment, while outside equity can affect control. Relevant risks and terms influence which finance is practical. The firm also needs working resources during the adjustment period: buying machinery without funds for materials or training may leave it idle. Explain the particular financing constraint rather than describing all small firms as lacking ambition or all large firms as having unlimited access to funds.
92	
93	### B-6145-5.4-011 Organisation determines how well size is handled
94	Larger operations can require clearer division of responsibility, delegation and information systems. A single owner may coordinate a small workshop directly but struggle to check every order across several sites. Appropriate organisation allows decisions to be made by people with relevant knowledge while keeping activities aligned. It can make a larger scale workable without requiring one person to perform every management task.
95	
96	If the invented tile firm opens several outlets without a shared stock record, stores may promise unavailable products or duplicate orders. Delays and rework add costs. A suitable stock system and clear responsibilities can address that particular problem, though installation and training also require resources. Organisation is therefore both a possible constraint and an area for improvement.
97	
98	Good organisation does not remove market and finance limits. Even an efficiently coordinated firm may remain small if customers want only a narrow range of customised work. Conversely, a large market does not ensure that a firm can manage rapid growth. The strongest judgement weighs market, capital and organisational conditions together, identifies the binding constraint and explains why a proposed change would ease it.

# 5.4 Economies and diseconomies of scale

## Notes

### B-6145-5.4-001 Classify the relationship before naming integration
Integration brings business activities under common ownership or control. It can occur when firms combine or one acquires another. To classify it, identify the original firm’s industry and production stage, then compare the acquired activity. Buying from a supplier under an ordinary contract is not by itself integration: the ownership or control relationship must change. Growth within an existing business is also distinct from combining previously separate firms.

Use an invented chain in Namibia: clay extraction supplies a tile manufacturer, which supplies a tile retailer serving households. The manufacturer is the reference point. Combining with another tile manufacturer is horizontal integration. Acquiring the retailer is forward vertical integration, moving towards the customer. Acquiring the clay supplier is backward vertical integration, moving towards the source of inputs. The direction follows the chain, not whether the acquired business is geographically north, nearer or larger.

Integration can change capacity, access to supplies or distribution, but the label does not prove success. Costs of acquisition, coordination and operation still matter. A larger combined firm may gain economies of scale while facing new management difficulties. Keep the classification question separate from the evaluation of cost consequences. A clear explanation first establishes the relationship and then examines the supplied benefits and limitations.

### B-6145-5.4-002 Horizontal: the same industry and stage
Horizontal integration combines firms at the same production stage in the same industry. If the invented Dune Tile Works acquires another tile manufacturer, both turn inputs into tiles at the manufacturing stage. Common ownership can combine production capacity, customers or distribution arrangements. Acquiring a supplier or retailer would be vertical rather than horizontal because the stage differs.

Potential cost gains could come from using a larger specialist machine, consolidating duplicated administration or negotiating purchases for a greater volume. These are possible consequences requiring evidence; they are not contained in the definition. Two factories operating separately under one owner may retain much of their previous cost structure. Integrating their records and processes can itself require resources.

To identify the type, ask whether the activities would have competed at the same stage before combination. Two tile manufacturers fit; a tile manufacturer and a tile shop do not, even though both concern tiles. Using the product alone as the test misses the stage distinction. A statement that a firm simply becomes larger is also insufficient to distinguish horizontal integration from expansion through new premises or vertical integration.

### B-6145-5.4-003 Forward: towards customers
Forward vertical integration combines an original firm with a later stage towards the final customer. When Dune Tile Works acquires its tile retailer, manufacturing is linked to retail distribution under common control. The manufacturer moves downstream in the production chain. It has not acquired another manufacturer, so the combination is not horizontal.

Direct control of retailing can improve access to customers or information about preferences. It may let the firm coordinate delivery and presentation more closely. However, it also requires retail skills, premises and stock management. A manufacturer’s technical experience does not automatically establish competence in selling to households. The likely benefit should be weighed against the resources needed to perform that later activity.

The reference point matters. Describe the original firm and the acquired stage rather than saying that ownership simply moves forward. Manufacturing followed by retailing is a sequence of activities, not a sequence determined by the date the businesses were founded. A manufacturer supplying an independent retailer remains a trading relationship unless the case states the relevant ownership or control change. This boundary makes the classification economically meaningful.

### B-6145-5.4-004 Backward: towards the inputs
Backward vertical integration combines an original firm with an earlier stage supplying its inputs. If Dune Tile Works acquires a clay extraction business, it extends ownership towards raw materials. The original manufacturer is still the reference point. The fact that clay eventually becomes a tile does not make its supplier the same manufacturing stage.

Control of a supplier may help coordinate deliveries or the required input quality. It can reduce dependence on an independent supplier if the acquired operation is reliable. Yet ownership does not remove extraction costs, geological limits or management problems. A previously competitive independent supply arrangement may even be cheaper than operating the supplier directly. Evaluate full costs rather than treating an internal transfer as a free input.

Compare the directions explicitly: retailer acquisition is forward from manufacturing, while input-supplier acquisition is backward. A useful classification states the activity acquired and its position in the chain. This prevents the common mistake of judging direction by the destination of money: a manufacturer pays its supplier, but the payment flow does not turn input acquisition into forward integration. The production sequence determines the label.

### B-6145-5.4-005 Economies of scale lower long-run average cost
Economies of scale are reductions in long-run average cost as production scale increases. In the long run the firm can adjust its scale and inputs rather than merely add workers to unchanged equipment. The cost benefit concerns the average per unit. Total cost can rise because much more is produced even while the unit cost falls. A bigger business is not evidence of an economy unless the relevant cost-per-unit mechanism is established.

Technical economies can arise when a larger operation makes efficient specialised equipment worthwhile. A small tile business may be unable to use a large kiln effectively; sustained larger output can make the technology economical. Managerial economies can arise when specialist purchasing or production managers improve decisions over an operation large enough to justify their employment. Both depend on the productive benefit exceeding the associated costs.

Purchasing economies may allow bulk discounts when suppliers’ savings or bargaining conditions support a lower input price. Financial economies can arise if a larger, well-established firm obtains more favourable finance under the stated risk conditions; lenders are not obliged to offer it cheaper credit merely because it is large. Marketing economies can spread an effective campaign’s cost over a larger sales volume. These are distinct routes to lower unit costs, not reasons to count the same saving repeatedly.

Internal economies come from growth of the individual firm. External economies come from growth of the industry outside that firm. A cluster of tile producers could attract specialist repair providers or training, improving access for participating firms. An individual firm can benefit without itself expanding. Identify whose growth causes the advantage before using internal or external.

For an original numerical illustration, imagine long-run output options of 100, 200 and 300 comparable units with average costs N$12, N$9 and N$8. These options permit adjustment of all inputs; they are not a fixed-kiln short-run schedule. To plot them, put output on the horizontal axis and long-run average cost in N$ per unit on the vertical axis. Mark the three labelled points. Their falling pattern illustrates economies over that range, while an explanation must still name the relevant technical, purchasing or other mechanism. The points alone do not prove which cause operates.

The distinction between firm and industry growth can be tested with a repair service. If Dune Tile Works expands enough to employ its own specialist kiln engineer efficiently, that is a potential internal managerial or technical advantage from its own scale. If several independent tile producers attract a nearby specialist repair business that serves them all, the improved access can be an external economy. In the second case, Dune Tile Works may benefit while its own output remains unchanged. The same useful service can therefore enter different explanations depending on the source of the advantage.

Risk sharing can also support a larger operation where it sells several products or reaches several markets. A fall in one source of sales may then have a smaller effect on total activity. This does not eliminate risk or directly demonstrate a unit-cost reduction; diversification adds coordination and may involve related demand changes. Explain the relevant saving or stability mechanism if a case relies on it rather than treating a longer product list as sufficient proof of economies.

### B-6145-5.4-006 Diseconomies of scale raise long-run average cost
Diseconomies of scale are increases in long-run average cost as production scale increases. An expanding organisation can become harder to coordinate. Messages passing through additional management layers may be delayed or distorted, leading to mismatched orders and waste. Departments may duplicate work or act on inconsistent information. If these problems add cost faster than they add useful output, unit cost rises.

Motivation can also weaken if workers feel remote from decisions or responsibility becomes unclear. Supervision and communication may then require more resources, with rework reducing usable output. These outcomes are possible organisational effects, not proof that large firms must be badly managed. Effective delegation and clear information can limit them. The task is to explain the supplied difficulty rather than make size itself an automatic cause.

External diseconomies arise when industry growth creates disadvantages outside one firm. For example, congestion on a shared access route can delay several producers, or competition for a scarce local input can raise its price. Distinguish these industry effects from a firm's internal communication problem. A single firm can experience external pressure even if its own scale is unchanged.

Extend the invented long-run illustration: output 300, 400 and 500 units has average cost N$8, N$9 and N$11. Plot output horizontally and long-run average cost vertically, marking the three points. The rising section illustrates diseconomies over that range. Combined with the earlier falling points, the schedule has its lowest listed average cost at 300. It does not establish an exact minimum between unlisted points.

Do not confuse this with diminishing returns. Diminishing returns concern adding a variable factor while another remains fixed, as when more workers share one unchanged kiln. Diseconomies concern larger long-run scale, where inputs can be adjusted. Both can be associated with rising costs, but the conditions and mechanisms differ. A classification must use those conditions rather than the upward direction of a cost figure alone.

### B-6145-5.4-007 Compare the net unit-cost effect
Expansion can create economies and diseconomies together. A larger order may secure cheaper materials while a more complex delivery system adds coordination costs. The net effect on long-run average cost depends on their relative size. Naming an economy does not prove the combined average cost falls; naming a management problem does not prove the whole expansion raises it.

Use invented per-unit changes with comparable output quality. Technical and purchasing gains save N$3 per unit, while additional coordination adds N$1. Net average cost falls N$2. In a more complex expansion, the same N$3 saving might be outweighed by N$4 added coordination cost, raising the average N$1. These calculations illustrate the balance rather than assigning a guaranteed cost pattern to a particular size.

Lower average cost can support profit at a given selling price when output is sold, but it is not sufficient to establish a profit increase in isolation. Prices, sales and total commitments also matter. Likewise, lower average cost does not mean the total resource bill falls. At 100 units with average cost N$12, total cost is N$1,200; at 300 with average cost N$8 it is N$2,400. The firm spends more in total while producing much more efficiently per unit.

A conclusion should therefore state the objective, the relevant scale range, the net cost effect and the sales condition. An expansion beyond the lowest listed unit-cost option might still have other attractions, but it cannot be justified as a unit-cost saving from this schedule. Keep the evidence and the proposed goal aligned.

Integration and economies of scale should not be used as synonyms. An acquisition changes ownership relationships; an economy of scale changes long-run average cost as scale increases. Integration may enable a saving, but it can also leave production arrangements largely unchanged or introduce costly duplication. A manufacturer acquiring its retailer gains a later-stage activity, not an automatic reduction in manufacturing cost. Trace how the combination affects resources and usable output before claiming the unit-cost benefit.

Where the data show lower average cost, test whether the compared products and quality are consistent. Producing smaller or less durable tiles can make a unit figure fall without an equivalent gain in satisfying customer requirements. The scale schedules here explicitly use comparable units so that the cost comparison concerns scale rather than a changed product. This condition belongs in any extension of the numerical argument.

### B-6145-5.4-008 Why firms differ in size
Firm size is influenced by the market it can serve, the capital it can secure and the organisation it can manage. Measures of size also differ: workers employed, sales, output and assets need not rank firms identically. A capital-intensive producer may have valuable equipment but relatively few workers. Use the stated measure rather than assuming size always means employment.

Small firms can remain viable through personal service, specialised products or flexibility. A customised tile restorer may serve a narrow local demand better with close customer contact than a large standardised operation would. Limited economies of scale can reduce the pressure to expand. The owner may also value control or lack the funds and organisation for growth.

These explanations interact. Capital can provide capacity without creating customers; a large market can offer opportunity without supplying finance; management can coordinate resources without guaranteeing sales. Compare the actual constraints in the case. A firm’s small current size is not by itself proof of inefficiency, just as a large current size is not proof that expansion has been successful.

### B-6145-5.4-009 Market size limits saleable output
A large sustained market can support sales needed to use larger-scale production efficiently. If confirmed customers want standard tiles in high volumes, equipment and specialist staff may be used sufficiently to justify expansion. Demand must be saleable at relevant prices, not merely a statement that people like the product. Willingness and ability to buy matter.

A narrow market may leave large equipment underused. An invented village producer of customised memorial tiles might have only a few orders each month. Building a large standard production plant would not create enough buyers by itself. Exporting or finding new markets could change the demand constraint, but those opportunities require evidence and may add transport or marketing costs.

Market stability matters as well as its current size. A temporary festival order might not support permanent capacity whose costs continue after the event. A stable stream of orders provides stronger support for sustained scale. When recommending growth, state why demand is expected to last and what would happen if sales weaken. This connects market size to feasible utilisation rather than treating expansion as an end in itself.

### B-6145-5.4-010 Capital available limits feasible expansion
Growth may need premises, machinery and funds for materials before customers pay. The economic resource capital includes produced means of production; finance enables the firm to acquire and operate them. A profitable-looking proposal can remain infeasible if the firm cannot secure the required funds on terms it can meet. Cash availability and expected profitability are related but different questions.

Suppose expansion requires an invented N$200,000 initial outlay while the owner can provide N$60,000 and no additional funding is currently available. The N$140,000 gap constrains that proposal even if a large market exists. A smaller staged expansion might fit the resources, while an outside investor or lender could change the position if willing to supply funds. Their willingness is not established merely by the owner wanting to grow.

Borrowing can create a repayment commitment, while outside equity can affect control. Relevant risks and terms influence which finance is practical. The firm also needs working resources during the adjustment period: buying machinery without funds for materials or training may leave it idle. Explain the particular financing constraint rather than describing all small firms as lacking ambition or all large firms as having unlimited access to funds.

### B-6145-5.4-011 Organisation determines how well size is handled
Larger operations can require clearer division of responsibility, delegation and information systems. A single owner may coordinate a small workshop directly but struggle to check every order across several sites. Appropriate organisation allows decisions to be made by people with relevant knowledge while keeping activities aligned. It can make a larger scale workable without requiring one person to perform every management task.

If the invented tile firm opens several outlets without a shared stock record, stores may promise unavailable products or duplicate orders. Delays and rework add costs. A suitable stock system and clear responsibilities can address that particular problem, though installation and training also require resources. Organisation is therefore both a possible constraint and an area for improvement.

Good organisation does not remove market and finance limits. Even an efficiently coordinated firm may remain small if customers want only a narrow range of customised work. Conversely, a large market does not ensure that a firm can manage rapid growth. The strongest judgement weighs market, capital and organisational conditions together, identifies the binding constraint and explains why a proposed change would ease it.

1	# 6.1 Government as producer and employer
2	
3	## Notes
4	
5	### B-6145-6.1-001 Separate production, provision and employment
6	Government participates in an economy by organising output and hiring people to help provide it. As a producer it creates goods or services; as an employer it purchases workers’ labour under employment arrangements. These roles can occur together. A government workshop making furniture may hire carpenters, while a government clinic may hire nurses to provide care. The furniture is a good and the care is a service, but each activity uses resources to satisfy wants.
7	
8	Ownership and output type answer different questions. Public sector identifies government control. Goods and services identify what is provided. A government-controlled organisation can produce tangible goods, and a private organisation can provide services. Likewise, a payment from government does not establish that government itself performed the production. It may purchase output from a private supplier. The supplied ownership, production and employment facts determine the description.
9	
10	Use an invented Namibian district throughout this topic. Its government workshop makes desks and storage cabinets, its clinic provides consultations, and its public library offers reading and lending services. The workshop employs carpenters; the clinic employs nurses; the library employs librarians. A separate privately owned courier delivers purchased supplies under a contract. These examples are hypothetical arrangements for identifying economic roles, rather than claims about the staffing of an actual institution.
11	
12	### B-6145-6.1-002 Government as a producer of goods
13	Goods are tangible outputs. In the invented district workshop, wood, tools, premises and skilled labour are organised to make desks and cabinets. Government controls the workshop’s production, so the case describes government production of goods. Identifying the desks alone describes the output; explaining the role also identifies the organisation producing them and the resources it uses.
14	
15	Producing these goods has an opportunity cost. Wood used for desks cannot simultaneously be used for another product, and carpenters’ time has alternative uses. Public ownership does not make the materials or labour unlimited. Even if a school receives a desk without paying a separate price, resources were needed to make it. Distinguish no direct payment by the recipient from no economic cost.
16	
17	If government instead buys ready-made desks from the private Reed Corner Workshop, the private workshop produces those desks and government purchases them. Government funding and government production are related but different roles. A question must state who actually makes the goods before the producer can be identified. The purchase can still support public provision of education, but that does not turn the independent workshop into a government organisation.
18	
19	The case may also state a production target rather than a sales target. A district workshop could be instructed to provide desks for public schools. This describes the purpose and destination of the output without proving that resources have been used efficiently. In this topic the immediate task is to recognise the production role, not assume a financial or social result absent from the evidence.
20	
21	### B-6145-6.1-003 Government as a provider of services
22	Services provide useful activities rather than a separately stored physical product. A clinic consultation, a lesson or a library lending service can satisfy wants while being delivered. Such output is production even though no factory makes an object. Government can organise these services through the organisations and workers it controls.
23	
24	The invented library uses librarians’ time, a building, records and equipment to help users access materials. The books are goods used in providing a service; the lending and assistance are service activities. This distinction prevents an explanation from calling the whole activity goods production merely because tangible objects are involved. A clinic similarly uses equipment and supplies while providing care.
25	
26	A service can be supplied without a direct user charge under a stated arrangement. That affects how access is financed, not whether scarce resources are consumed. Suppose an invented weekly library budget is N$4,000, including staff and operating resources, while users pay no lending fee. It is free at the point of use in that arrangement but still has a resource cost. The N$4,000 could have alternative uses.
27	
28	Government may fund a service delivered by a private provider or provide it through its own staff. Read the case before identifying the producer and employer. Topic 6.2 considers government policy choices and financing, while this topic establishes the distinct roles. No assumption about the current legal entitlement to a particular service is needed to describe the invented provision accurately.
29	
30	### B-6145-6.1-004 Government as an employer
31	Government acts as an employer when it hires workers for duties in its organisations. The invented district workshop’s carpenters and library’s librarians are direct government employees because the case states who employs them. Their work helps create goods or provide services. Wages are payments for labour, while the produced output is a separate part of the activity.
32	
33	An employee’s occupation alone does not identify the sector. A carpenter can work for a government workshop, a private firm or independently. A nurse can work for different kinds of provider. Establish the employment relationship rather than inferring government employment from the job title. The person or organisation making employment decisions and paying wages under the stated contract is relevant.
34	
35	The private courier’s drivers remain employees of the courier when delivering supplies to the district. Government buys the delivery service from the contractor; it does not directly employ those drivers in the supplied arrangement. This boundary matters when describing the size or role of public employment. Counting everyone whose work eventually serves a public organisation would overstate direct government employment.
36	
37	### B-6145-6.1-005 Public provision, public goods and free goods
38	A public good in the economic sense is non-rival and non-excludable: one person’s use does not reduce availability to another, and preventing non-payers from benefiting is difficult. A free good has no opportunity cost in the relevant circumstances. Neither definition means simply something government supplies without charging the user.
39	
40	The invented workshop’s desks use scarce materials and labour, so they are economic goods even if supplied without a school purchase charge. A library service also uses scarce staff time and premises. Public provision describes the institutional arrangement; classifying a public good requires the non-rivalry and non-excludability tests. Keep these tests separate from whether an organisation is public sector. Topic 1.1 owns the underlying scarcity distinction, which continues to apply when government provides the output.
41

# 6.1 Government as producer and employer

## Notes

### B-6145-6.1-001 Separate production, provision and employment
Government participates in an economy by organising output and hiring people to help provide it. As a producer it creates goods or services; as an employer it purchases workers’ labour under employment arrangements. These roles can occur together. A government workshop making furniture may hire carpenters, while a government clinic may hire nurses to provide care. The furniture is a good and the care is a service, but each activity uses resources to satisfy wants.

Ownership and output type answer different questions. Public sector identifies government control. Goods and services identify what is provided. A government-controlled organisation can produce tangible goods, and a private organisation can provide services. Likewise, a payment from government does not establish that government itself performed the production. It may purchase output from a private supplier. The supplied ownership, production and employment facts determine the description.

Use an invented Namibian district throughout this topic. Its government workshop makes desks and storage cabinets, its clinic provides consultations, and its public library offers reading and lending services. The workshop employs carpenters; the clinic employs nurses; the library employs librarians. A separate privately owned courier delivers purchased supplies under a contract. These examples are hypothetical arrangements for identifying economic roles, rather than claims about the staffing of an actual institution.

### B-6145-6.1-002 Government as a producer of goods
Goods are tangible outputs. In the invented district workshop, wood, tools, premises and skilled labour are organised to make desks and cabinets. Government controls the workshop’s production, so the case describes government production of goods. Identifying the desks alone describes the output; explaining the role also identifies the organisation producing them and the resources it uses.

Producing these goods has an opportunity cost. Wood used for desks cannot simultaneously be used for another product, and carpenters’ time has alternative uses. Public ownership does not make the materials or labour unlimited. Even if a school receives a desk without paying a separate price, resources were needed to make it. Distinguish no direct payment by the recipient from no economic cost.

If government instead buys ready-made desks from the private Reed Corner Workshop, the private workshop produces those desks and government purchases them. Government funding and government production are related but different roles. A question must state who actually makes the goods before the producer can be identified. The purchase can still support public provision of education, but that does not turn the independent workshop into a government organisation.

The case may also state a production target rather than a sales target. A district workshop could be instructed to provide desks for public schools. This describes the purpose and destination of the output without proving that resources have been used efficiently. In this topic the immediate task is to recognise the production role, not assume a financial or social result absent from the evidence.

### B-6145-6.1-003 Government as a provider of services
Services provide useful activities rather than a separately stored physical product. A clinic consultation, a lesson or a library lending service can satisfy wants while being delivered. Such output is production even though no factory makes an object. Government can organise these services through the organisations and workers it controls.

The invented library uses librarians’ time, a building, records and equipment to help users access materials. The books are goods used in providing a service; the lending and assistance are service activities. This distinction prevents an explanation from calling the whole activity goods production merely because tangible objects are involved. A clinic similarly uses equipment and supplies while providing care.

A service can be supplied without a direct user charge under a stated arrangement. That affects how access is financed, not whether scarce resources are consumed. Suppose an invented weekly library budget is N$4,000, including staff and operating resources, while users pay no lending fee. It is free at the point of use in that arrangement but still has a resource cost. The N$4,000 could have alternative uses.

Government may fund a service delivered by a private provider or provide it through its own staff. Read the case before identifying the producer and employer. Topic 6.2 considers government policy choices and financing, while this topic establishes the distinct roles. No assumption about the current legal entitlement to a particular service is needed to describe the invented provision accurately.

### B-6145-6.1-004 Government as an employer
Government acts as an employer when it hires workers for duties in its organisations. The invented district workshop’s carpenters and library’s librarians are direct government employees because the case states who employs them. Their work helps create goods or provide services. Wages are payments for labour, while the produced output is a separate part of the activity.

An employee’s occupation alone does not identify the sector. A carpenter can work for a government workshop, a private firm or independently. A nurse can work for different kinds of provider. Establish the employment relationship rather than inferring government employment from the job title. The person or organisation making employment decisions and paying wages under the stated contract is relevant.

The private courier’s drivers remain employees of the courier when delivering supplies to the district. Government buys the delivery service from the contractor; it does not directly employ those drivers in the supplied arrangement. This boundary matters when describing the size or role of public employment. Counting everyone whose work eventually serves a public organisation would overstate direct government employment.

### B-6145-6.1-005 Public provision, public goods and free goods
A public good in the economic sense is non-rival and non-excludable: one person’s use does not reduce availability to another, and preventing non-payers from benefiting is difficult. A free good has no opportunity cost in the relevant circumstances. Neither definition means simply something government supplies without charging the user.

The invented workshop’s desks use scarce materials and labour, so they are economic goods even if supplied without a school purchase charge. A library service also uses scarce staff time and premises. Public provision describes the institutional arrangement; classifying a public good requires the non-rivalry and non-excludability tests. Keep these tests separate from whether an organisation is public sector. Topic 1.1 owns the underlying scarcity distinction, which continues to apply when government provides the output.
