# 6.3 Government control

## Notes

### B-6145-6.3-001 Identify the problem the intervention addresses
A business considers its own receipts and costs, but its decisions can affect other people. An external cost is a cost imposed on third parties that is not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s private cost. If an invented workshop releases dust that damages neighbouring gardens, the neighbours bear a cost even though they did not buy or produce the workshop’s output. An intervention can seek to reduce that harm or make the producer take more of it into account.

Other reasons include unsafe products, misleading information and unfair treatment. Consumers may be unable to inspect a food product’s safety before buying it. Workers may lack the information or bargaining strength to secure safe conditions individually. A clear standard and effective inspection can reduce these problems, but the proposed control should address the actual cause rather than merely restrict activity.

Intervention uses resources too. Inspectors need skills and time, firms may need new equipment, and a poorly designed rule can discourage useful output. These costs do not prove intervention is undesirable; they belong in the comparison with the harm prevented. Explain the market problem, the mechanism and the implementation condition before making a judgement. A rule written down is not equivalent to a harmful practice being eliminated.

An external cost should also be separated from an ordinary private expense. The workshop’s payment for its own materials is already borne by the business. The neighbours’ damaged plants are different because they are affected third parties. If a cleaner process costs the firm more but prevents substantial third-party damage, the private cost increase alone does not establish a worse social result. The assessment includes effects outside the firm’s accounts.

### B-6145-6.3-002 Production controls change constraints and incentives
Standards can specify acceptable product or process requirements. Inspection can check compliance, while a licence can require stated conditions before an activity is permitted. Restrictions can limit particularly harmful production. A tax on a harmful activity can increase its private cost, encouraging reduction or a cleaner alternative where a response is feasible. A subsidy can encourage a socially useful activity but requires funding and a way to target the intended behaviour.

At the invented Garden Ridge Food Workshop, a proposed hygiene standard requires clean storage and safe handling. Inspection checks actual practice rather than relying solely on the seller’s assurance. If breaches are detected and correction is required under the supplied arrangement, the producer has an incentive to improve. The mechanism is more convincing with clear requirements, reliable checks and practical ways to comply.

Control can affect cost, output and prices. Installing safe equipment uses resources; unsafe low-cost methods may no longer be allowed. Some costs may be passed to buyers depending on demand and competition. The relevant comparison includes improved safety and harm avoided, not just the firm’s immediate outlay. Conversely, a vague requirement or infrequent monitoring can leave the original problem unresolved despite formal compliance claims. Use the particular rule in a case; no current statutory penalty or licensing requirement is invented here.

### B-6145-6.3-003 Consumer protection in Namibia
Consumers need information and reasonably safe products to make useful choices. Accurate descriptions, measures and warnings can reduce misleading impressions; standards and testing can check characteristics not visible at purchase. A complaint mechanism can allow a reported defect to be investigated and an appropriate remedy considered. These measures complement rather than replace consumers’ ability to compare offers.

In Namibia, the [Namibian Standards Institution](https://www.nsi.com.na/inspection/) describes product, facility and process inspection supporting quality and food safety. This provides a concrete institutional example without assuming that every product has been inspected or certified. A conformity claim must relate to the relevant product and assessment, not be treated as a blanket guarantee of all future performance.

Consider an invented sealed-food purchase where the buyer cannot observe contamination. Reliable sampling and process checks can detect hazards the buyer cannot identify. Clear labels can communicate storage instructions. Accessible complaint routes can reveal recurring problems. Their value depends on appropriate tests, competent inspection, correction and consumers knowing how to report concerns.

Compliance and enforcement have costs. Small producers may need training or improved facilities, and inspection capacity can be limited. These constraints strengthen the case for clear, workable requirements and risk-focused enforcement rather than a claim that protection has no cost. The judgement should weigh harm prevented against resources used and ask whether the mechanism actually reaches the products and consumers at risk.

Information and enforcement have complementary roles. A label describing safe storage cannot correct contamination already present in the sealed product. Testing can investigate that hazard but cannot ensure a buyer follows storage instructions afterwards. In the invented case, combining appropriate process checks with clear information addresses different stages of the risk. Calling either measure sufficient on its own would overlook the particular problem it cannot solve. A complaint record can then help identify repeated failures and direct scarce inspection effort, provided reports are investigated fairly rather than treated as proven automatically.

### B-6145-6.3-004 Employee protection and practical enforcement
Employees have interests in safe work, fair treatment and fulfilment of stated employment terms. Protection can operate through rules, inspection, information, representation and dispute processes. Safety requirements can encourage guards on dangerous equipment or changes to hazardous processes. Clear records and accessible complaints can help identify failures in agreed pay or conditions. The exact legal entitlement must come from the applicable rule rather than an invented number.

Namibia’s [Labour Services directorate](https://mol.gov.na/division-of-labour-services) describes employment-condition inspection and occupational safety and health functions. These are mechanisms for monitoring and enforcing protection. They do not establish that all workplaces comply, nor that a complaint automatically produces a particular award. Investigation, evidence and follow-up affect the result.

Use an invented machine workshop where a guard is missing and workers fear reporting it. A clear safety requirement can establish the expected condition, but workers also need a trusted reporting route and a prompt response. Inspection followed by effective correction can reduce exposure to injury. A poster alone is weaker if the hazard remains and complaints cannot safely be raised.

Employers bear compliance costs, but injuries can also impose lost time, damage and costs on workers and others. An evaluation should compare these consequences and the feasibility of correction. Limited inspectors or poor records can delay protection. Support for awareness and practical compliance can improve effectiveness, while no prediction should assume perfect enforcement merely because an agency has a stated mandate.

Follow-up can check whether the guard was actually fitted and remains usable. Recording an instruction to repair it is a different outcome from removing the continuing hazard.

### B-6145-6.3-005 HIV and AIDS: protect people without status-based assumptions
Workplace protection can address discrimination, misuse of personal health information and exclusion from fair opportunities. HIV status alone is not proof that a person cannot perform a job. Decisions should be grounded in relevant work circumstances rather than stigma. Topic 5.2 considers actual health-related productivity effects; that is a different question from denying opportunities merely because of a person’s status.

The [ILO HIV and AIDS Recommendation](https://www.ilo.org/dyn/normlex/en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:12100:0::NO::P12100_ILO_CODE:R200) supports non-discrimination and confidentiality principles. As a protection approach, government can support clear workplace policies, education and accessible complaint arrangements, with monitoring of unfair treatment. This does not require inventing a domestic testing rule, penalty or disclosure procedure. International guidance and an enforceable domestic entitlement are distinct kinds of evidence.

In an invented workplace, confidential handling of a complaint can help an affected worker seek assistance without unnecessary disclosure. Education can challenge incorrect assumptions, while a fair review can examine actual employment decisions. A policy is less effective if workers fear retaliation, supervisors are unaware of it or sensitive information is shared unnecessarily. Trust and follow-up therefore matter alongside the written statement.

Protection should be evaluated with practical constraints. Training and complaint handling use resources, and workers may not know their options. A combined approach can be stronger than a statement alone if it is accessible and consistently applied. The conclusion should connect non-discrimination, appropriate privacy and effective implementation, while keeping the worker’s actual capacity and individual circumstances separate from assumptions based on HIV status.

1	# 7.1 Prices
2	
3	## Notes
4	
5	### B-6145-7.1-001 Measure a basket against its base
6	A retail price index summarises changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket compared with a base period. A basket contains specified quantities of goods and services. Holding quantities fixed in a simple example separates price changes from changes in what is purchased. The base index is set to 100; it is a reference number rather than a money amount.
7	
8	Use an invented Namibian household basket costing N$500 in the base year, N$550 in Year 1 and N$577.50 in Year 2. The simple index is current basket cost / base basket cost × 100. This distinguishes a change in index points from a percentage change. Basket selection, quality changes and changing consumption patterns can affect the usefulness of the measure. In a simple calculation use the supplied comparable basket rather than introducing unprovided quantities or treating the index as a precise experience shared by every household.
13

If A rises to N$12 while B stays N$20, the same quantities cost N$220, giving an index of 110. Simply averaging the two percentage price changes would give a different result because their contributions to expenditure need not be equal. Cost the specified quantities first.

17	Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. A single product becoming dearer does not establish that general pattern; other prices could be unchanged or falling. Demand-pull inflation begins with demand growing beyond what firms can readily supply. Buyers compete for limited available output, putting upward pressure on prices. The capacity condition matters: stronger demand can instead raise real output where resources are idle and supply responds.
18	
19	Cost-push inflation begins with increased production costs, such as a broad rise in imported input prices. If firms pass those costs into selling prices, the general level can rise even without stronger consumer demand. The cost increase must spread sufficiently to support a general-price explanation; one workshop’s isolated bill is not the whole economy. The two causes can operate together, so identify the initiating change and the evidence rather than assuming a single cause.

Deflation would mean a sustained decline in the general price level. # 7.1 Prices

## Notes

### B-6145-7.1-001 Measure a basket against its base
A retail price index summarises changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket compared with a base period. A basket contains specified quantities of goods and services. Holding quantities fixed in a simple example separates price changes from changes in what is purchased. The base index is set to 100; it is a reference number rather than a money amount.

Use an invented Namibian household basket costing N$500 in the base year, N$550 in Year 1 and N$577.50 in Year 2. The simple index is current basket cost / base basket cost × 100. Year 1 gives 550 / 500 × 100 = 110; Year 2 gives 577.50 / 500 × 100 = 115.5. An index of 115.5 means the same basket costs 15.5% more than in the base year.

The annual change from Year 1 is not 15.5%. The index rises 5.5 points from 110 to 115.5. Dividing 5.5 by the earlier 110 gives 0.05, equivalent to 5%. This distinguishes a change in index points from a percentage change. Similarly, the base-to-Year-1 rise is 10%, so the annual inflation rate slows from 10% to 5% even though the basket keeps becoming more expensive.

A representative basket is an average. A household buying more of the fastest-rising items can experience a larger increase in its own cost of living. Basket selection, quality changes and changing consumption patterns can affect the usefulness of the measure. In a simple calculation use the supplied comparable basket rather than introducing unprovided quantities or treating the index as a precise experience shared by every household.

Basket costs can be built from individual prices and quantities. An invented basket containing ten units of item A and five of item B costs N$200 if A is N$10 and B N$20. If A rises to N$12 while B stays N$20, the same quantities cost N$220, giving an index of 110. Simply averaging the two percentage price changes would give a different result because their contributions to expenditure need not be equal. Cost the specified quantities first.

### B-6145-7.1-002 Distinguish the price trend from its cause
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. A single product becoming dearer does not establish that general pattern; other prices could be unchanged or falling. Demand-pull inflation begins with demand growing beyond what firms can readily supply. Buyers compete for limited available output, putting upward pressure on prices. The capacity condition matters: stronger demand can instead raise real output where resources are idle and supply responds.

Cost-push inflation begins with increased production costs, such as a broad rise in imported input prices. If firms pass those costs into selling prices, the general level can rise even without stronger consumer demand. The cost increase must spread sufficiently to support a general-price explanation; one workshop’s isolated bill is not the whole economy. The two causes can operate together, so identify the initiating change and the evidence rather than assuming a single cause.

Slower positive inflation is disinflation, not deflation. In the invented basket, prices still rise in Year 2 despite the slower rate. Deflation would mean a sustained decline in the general price level. These distinctions affect a household’s interpretation: a lower inflation announcement does not promise restoration of the previous year’s prices. Topic 6.2 considers policy instruments; this topic owns the measurement, causes and consequences.

### B-6145-7.1-003 Consequences depend on incomes, contracts and expectations
If an invented pension stays N$3,000 while the pensioner’s basket prices rise 10%, the same money buys less. To buy the old bundle would require N$3,300. The purchasing-power loss follows from income failing to adjust, not from the pension’s money amount falling. A household whose income rises with relevant prices may avoid that particular loss, although its personal basket and timing still matter.

Inflation can affect savers and lenders where returns fail to compensate for higher prices. A fixed money balance can buy less later. A debtor with a fixed nominal sum can owe less in real purchasing-power terms after unexpected inflation. Yet the nominal debt remains due, and the debtor’s repayment burden relative to income improves only if income rises or other relevant conditions change. A person with fixed income and rising essentials can find repayment harder despite lower real debt value.

Uncertain inflation can complicate budgets, pricing and investment decisions. Businesses may struggle to distinguish a general price rise from demand for their own product. Competitiveness can weaken if domestic costs and export prices rise faster than competitors’ without offsetting productivity or exchange-rate changes. These are conditional effects, not proof that each firm’s profit falls.

Anticipated low stable inflation can be easier to plan for than an unexpected rapid rise. Contracts may adjust, and some workers may negotiate higher pay. The judgement should compare the affected groups and their ability to adapt. Fixed-income households face a strong direct purchasing-power risk; debtors can gain in real terms under a fixed nominal contract, but income, prices and financing conditions decide practical affordability. No group label alone settles the outcome.

Relative price changes can alter the effect further. A business selling a product whose price is rising may still face input costs increasing faster, squeezing its margin. Another can pass costs on more readily. Inflation is a general measure, so an individual profit conclusion needs both receipts and costs rather than the general rate alone.

8	Use invented employment figures. In Year 1 agriculture employs 200 people and services 300, giving 500 in total. In Year 2 agriculture employs 220 and services 380, giving 600. Agricultural employment rises by 20, yet its share falls from 40% to about 36.67%. Services grow faster. Describing agriculture as losing jobs because its share fell would confuse the relative pattern with the absolute level.
9	
10	Changing customer demand, technology and skills can change occupational requirements. More machines can reduce demand for a manual task and raise demand for maintenance skills. The net job effect depends on those changes and the output sold. Full-time, part-time and self-employed work can also change differently, so a headcount alone may hide a change in hours or security.
11	
12	A simple unemployment rate divides unemployed people by the labour force, employed plus unemployed under the specified definition. If 600 are employed and 100 unemployed, the labour force is 700 and the rate about 14.29%. Children and people outside the labour force are not added to the denominator merely because they are residents. Use a consistent measure before comparing periods, since changed definitions or search behaviour can affect the figures.
13	
14	### B-6145-7.2-002 Identify the cause rather than assume unwillingness
15	Unemployment concerns people without work who are willing and able to work and seeking employment under the stated measure. A person studying full-time without seeking work is not automatically unemployed. Nor does unemployment alone show unwillingness to work: an employer may have no vacancy, or available jobs may require different skills. The relevant evidence is the labour-market situation.
16	
17	Cyclical or demand-deficient unemployment can follow a broad fall in orders. Firms reduce output and labour demand even when workers have useful skills. Structural unemployment arises when the pattern of jobs changes and workers’ skills or location do not match available vacancies. Technological unemployment is one possible structural case when equipment replaces particular tasks and displaced workers cannot readily fill new roles.
18	
19	Seasonal unemployment arises when work is available only during part of the year, such as a supplied harvesting period. Frictional unemployment reflects time spent finding and moving into a suitable job. These cases need different explanations: a search delay differs from a permanent skill mismatch or a broad absence of buyers. More than one cause can affect the same person.
20	
21	For example, an invented packing plant loses orders during a general spending decline and dismisses workers who could perform the former tasks. Demand support addresses a different problem from retraining a worker whose former task has permanently changed while suitable new vacancies exist. 22	
23	### B-6145-7.2-003 Follow the consequences to households and the economy
24	Losing a job can reduce earned income and the ability to meet household spending commitments. Existing savings, another household income or support can cushion the immediate effect, but they are not guaranteed or unlimited. A household may reduce discretionary purchases first, while essential bills remain difficult to adjust. Reduced purchases can also weaken orders at other businesses if the spending loss is not offset elsewhere.
25	
26	Unused willing and suitable labour represents potential output forgone when productive opportunities exist. Tax revenue may fall as earnings and spending decline, while support needs can increase. The fiscal effect depends on the tax and benefit arrangements supplied; no automatic payment or exact current amount is assumed. These are economy-wide channels rather than simply a cost shown in one employer’s accounts.
27	
28	Long unemployment may allow skills to deteriorate or make it harder to maintain contacts and confidence. This can weaken later recruitment prospects, reinforcing the original loss. Short search unemployment need not have the same lasting effect. Duration and access to training matter when comparing consequences.
29	
30	An invented closure removing 30 jobs at one plant is a gross local loss. If other businesses employ 20 of the affected workers during the same period, the net position differs from assuming all 30 remain unemployed. Relocation can still impose costs and the replacement jobs may differ in hours or pay. Assess both the net numbers and the individual circumstances rather than assuming a job replacement removes every consequence.
31	
32	### B-6145-7.2-004 Match the remedy to the binding cause
33	Training can help workers meet actual vacancies requiring new skills. It is more convincing when the course is relevant, affordable and accessible and employers genuinely need the skill. Training takes time and does not create customers by itself. If most firms face weak demand, newly qualified workers may still lack vacancies. Job information and placement support can instead reduce search delays where suitable vacancies already exist.
34	
35	Demand support, such as feasible funded public purchases, can help where suitable workers and capacity are idle because orders are weak. It may create output and jobs if resources respond. Its limits include financing, implementation delays, imports and price pressure when capacity is tight. Topic 6.2 explains those policy channels; the present task is matching them to the unemployment cause.
36	
37	Mobility support can help where vacancies are elsewhere, but housing, transport and family commitments affect feasibility. Occupational mobility can require training; geographical mobility concerns location. Seasonal diversification can provide work outside the main production season if demand for the alternative output exists. A calendar change does not itself create that demand.
38	
39	Evaluate a remedy through cause, mechanism, cost and time. For a skill mismatch with unfilled vacancies, relevant training is well targeted. For a general fall in demand with unchanged useful skills, demand support is more direct, provided it is affordable and capacity can respond. A combination may be needed where both problems exist. A conditional choice grounded in the actual constraint is stronger than declaring one remedy best for all unemployed people.
40	
41	Check additionality when counting the benefit. A programme hiring 50 people may replace existing work or draw some recruits from other employers. Its gross places are not automatically 50 extra jobs for the economy. Similarly, a completed course is not itself evidence of later employment. Relevant follow-up would compare actual placement into sustained suitable work, including the time needed to obtain it.
42	
43	Measures can also complement each other. Information about genuine vacancies can help a trained worker find a match, while affordable transport can make that match feasible. Where those barriers coexist, improving skills alone may leave the last obstacle intact. Diagnose the sequence of constraints before deciding which resources to spend.
44	
45	The relevant comparison is sustained suitable employment, including the actual hours and earnings, rather than course attendance or announced vacancies alone.

# 7.2 Employment

## Notes

### B-6145-7.2-001 Describe levels and patterns separately
Employment is work used in producing goods and services. Its level is the number employed, while its pattern concerns how jobs are distributed across sectors, occupations, places and working arrangements. Growth in services can coexist with declining manufacturing employment, or both can grow at different rates. A statement about one share does not establish the direction of the total.

Use invented employment figures. In Year 1 agriculture employs 200 people and services 300, giving 500 in total. In Year 2 agriculture employs 220 and services 380, giving 600. Agricultural employment rises by 20, yet its share falls from 40% to about 36.67%. Services grow faster. Describing agriculture as losing jobs because its share fell would confuse the relative pattern with the absolute level.

Changing customer demand, technology and skills can change occupational requirements. More machines can reduce demand for a manual task and raise demand for maintenance skills. The net job effect depends on those changes and the output sold. Full-time, part-time and self-employed work can also change differently, so a headcount alone may hide a change in hours or security.

A simple unemployment rate divides unemployed people by the labour force, employed plus unemployed under the specified definition. If 600 are employed and 100 unemployed, the labour force is 700 and the rate about 14.29%. Children and people outside the labour force are not added to the denominator merely because they are residents. Use a consistent measure before comparing periods, since changed definitions or search behaviour can affect the figures.

### B-6145-7.2-002 Identify the cause rather than assume unwillingness
Unemployment concerns people without work who are willing and able to work and seeking employment under the stated measure. A person studying full-time without seeking work is not automatically unemployed. Nor does unemployment alone show unwillingness to work: an employer may have no vacancy, or available jobs may require different skills. The relevant evidence is the labour-market situation.

Cyclical or demand-deficient unemployment can follow a broad fall in orders. Firms reduce output and labour demand even when workers have useful skills. Structural unemployment arises when the pattern of jobs changes and workers’ skills or location do not match available vacancies. Technological unemployment is one possible structural case when equipment replaces particular tasks and displaced workers cannot readily fill new roles.

Seasonal unemployment arises when work is available only during part of the year, such as a supplied harvesting period. Frictional unemployment reflects time spent finding and moving into a suitable job. These cases need different explanations: a search delay differs from a permanent skill mismatch or a broad absence of buyers. More than one cause can affect the same person.

For example, an invented packing plant loses orders during a general spending decline and dismisses workers who could perform the former tasks. Demand support addresses a different problem from retraining a worker whose former task has permanently changed while suitable new vacancies exist. Neither case is diagnosed from the unemployment label alone. Name the initiating change and the reason it reduces access to paid work.

### B-6145-7.2-003 Follow the consequences to households and the economy
Losing a job can reduce earned income and the ability to meet household spending commitments. Existing savings, another household income or support can cushion the immediate effect, but they are not guaranteed or unlimited. A household may reduce discretionary purchases first, while essential bills remain difficult to adjust. Reduced purchases can also weaken orders at other businesses if the spending loss is not offset elsewhere.

Unused willing and suitable labour represents potential output forgone when productive opportunities exist. Tax revenue may fall as earnings and spending decline, while support needs can increase. The fiscal effect depends on the tax and benefit arrangements supplied; no automatic payment or exact current amount is assumed. These are economy-wide channels rather than simply a cost shown in one employer’s accounts.

Long unemployment may allow skills to deteriorate or make it harder to maintain contacts and confidence. This can weaken later recruitment prospects, reinforcing the original loss. Short search unemployment need not have the same lasting effect. Duration and access to training matter when comparing consequences.

An invented closure removing 30 jobs at one plant is a gross local loss. If other businesses employ 20 of the affected workers during the same period, the net position differs from assuming all 30 remain unemployed. Relocation can still impose costs and the replacement jobs may differ in hours or pay. Assess both the net numbers and the individual circumstances rather than assuming a job replacement removes every consequence.

### B-6145-7.2-004 Match the remedy to the binding cause
Training can help workers meet actual vacancies requiring new skills. It is more convincing when the course is relevant, affordable and accessible and employers genuinely need the skill. Training takes time and does not create customers by itself. If most firms face weak demand, newly qualified workers may still lack vacancies. Job information and placement support can instead reduce search delays where suitable vacancies already exist.

Demand support, such as feasible funded public purchases, can help where suitable workers and capacity are idle because orders are weak. It may create output and jobs if resources respond. Its limits include financing, implementation delays, imports and price pressure when capacity is tight. Topic 6.2 explains those policy channels; the present task is matching them to the unemployment cause.

Mobility support can help where vacancies are elsewhere, but housing, transport and family commitments affect feasibility. Occupational mobility can require training; geographical mobility concerns location. Seasonal diversification can provide work outside the main production season if demand for the alternative output exists. A calendar change does not itself create that demand.

Evaluate a remedy through cause, mechanism, cost and time. For a skill mismatch with unfilled vacancies, relevant training is well targeted. For a general fall in demand with unchanged useful skills, demand support is more direct, provided it is affordable and capacity can respond. A combination may be needed where both problems exist. A conditional choice grounded in the actual constraint is stronger than declaring one remedy best for all unemployed people.

Check additionality when counting the benefit. A programme hiring 50 people may replace existing work or draw some recruits from other employers. Its gross places are not automatically 50 extra jobs for the economy. Similarly, a completed course is not itself evidence of later employment. Relevant follow-up would compare actual placement into sustained suitable work, including the time needed to obtain it.

Measures can also complement each other. Information about genuine vacancies can help a trained worker find a match, while affordable transport can make that match feasible. 1	# 7.3 Output
2	
3	## Notes
4	
5	### B-6145-7.3-001 Domestic, national and income describe different boundaries
6	National accounts measure production and the incomes and spending associated with it over a period. Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, concerns production within the territory. Gross National Product, or GNP, adjusts domestic product for net income earned from abroad by residents under the stated convention. National Income concerns income earned by a country’s factors of production. The names are related, but they do not permit every figure to be substituted for another without checking its definition.
7	
8	Specify the period and basis before comparing. A monthly current-price total and an annual constant-price figure answer different questions. Domestic and national boundaries can differ where residents earn abroad or non-residents earn within the country. Gross and net measures also differ where capital-consumption allowance is deducted. These distinctions prevent a meaningful definition from becoming an unsupported numerical equality.
9	
10	The simple invented cases below isolate one distinction at a time. They do not claim that current published national accounts contain no further adjustments. Where a question states a particular accounting convention, use it consistently and describe the measure actually obtained. Topic 5.3 measures an individual firm’s costs and revenue; the national account combines activity across producers while preventing repeated counting of the same production.
11	
12	### B-6145-7.3-002 GDP: production inside the territory
13	Gross Domestic Product is the value of final goods and services produced within a country’s territory over a specified period, avoiding double counting. Final refers to output used for final consumption or investment rather than an input whose value is already included in another product. Services count alongside tangible goods. A year’s GDP is a flow of production, not the stock of wealth or cash balances at one date.
14	
15	The domestic boundary follows location. If an invented non-resident-owned factory produces furniture inside Namibia, that production contributes to domestic output. Whether its owners later receive income abroad is relevant to a national-income adjustment, not a reason to erase the factory’s domestic production. Conversely, a resident’s production abroad does not become domestic output merely because the resident has a Namibian connection.
16	
17	Current-price GDP values output at the prices of the period. It can rise because more is produced, prices rise or both. A real or constant-price comparison holds the price effect apart so changes in production can be examined. If the same quantities are valued 10% higher solely because prices rise, that is not evidence of a 10% expansion in real output.
18	
19	GDP also differs from total sales of every producer added without adjustment. A material can be sold to a manufacturer and its value appear again in the final product. Counting both full values would repeat the intermediate component. The output method addresses that problem through value added, while the expenditure method focuses on final purchases.
20	
21	### B-6145-7.3-003 GNP: adjust for net income from abroad
22	GNP adjusts domestic product for net factor income from abroad under the course’s stated convention. Add relevant income received from abroad by residents and subtract corresponding income paid to non-residents. Net means the difference between these opposing flows. It does not mean simply adding whichever foreign receipt is mentioned and ignoring payments outward.
23	
24	Use invented annual figures in N$ million. Domestic product is 1,000, factor income received from abroad is 70 and factor income paid abroad is 90. Net income from abroad is 70 minus 90, or negative 20. GNP is therefore 980 on this specified basis. A negative net figure makes the national measure smaller than the domestic measure; it is not added as a positive 20.
25	
26	The adjustment concerns factor income, not the trade balance. Exports and imports are purchases of output, while a factor-income flow is a reward from productive resources. An imported machine and a resident’s foreign interest receipt belong to different transactions. Their shared international character does not make them interchangeable in the adjustment.
27	
28	Residence is also different from citizenship alone. The relevant national-accounting boundary concerns residents and their income under the stated convention. Do not decide inclusion merely from a passport description where the question supplies residence and production facts. The simple adjustment clarifies the domestic-national distinction without requiring an unsupported claim that every transfer from abroad is factor income.
29	
30	### B-6145-7.3-004 National Income: earnings from production
31	National Income concerns the income earned by a country’s factors of production over a stated period. Wages reward labour; rent, interest and profit are other factor-income categories in the elementary treatment. The focus is earned income associated with production rather than every receipt of money. A transfer received without supplying current goods or services in exchange is not newly earned factor income.
32	
33	Suppose an invented production example generates N$600 wages, N$100 rent, N$50 interest and N$250 profit, with all categories mutually exclusive and all relevant factor incomes included. Their sum is N$1,000. A separate N$80 support transfer to a household should not be added as new production income. It reallocates purchasing power rather than creating another N$80 of output.
34	
35	The exact National Income measure depends on the accounting basis. A gross output value, a net income value and a value including product taxes need not be identical without adjustments. Gross means before capital-consumption allowance is deducted; net means after the relevant capital-consumption allowance adjustment. Use the convention supplied rather than inventing a bridge from one headline figure to another. The simple factor-income example sets aside such adjustments explicitly.
36	
37	This discipline also helps prevent double counting profits. If wages have already been subtracted in arriving at the stated profit, adding wages and that profit counts different shares of value added. Adding sales receipts again would repeat the income generated by the same output. A household’s receipt and subsequent spending are connected stages, not two separate additions to National Income.
38	
39	### B-6145-7.3-005 Three views of the same productive activity
40	The output method looks at what is produced or the value added by producers. The income method looks at the factor earnings generated. The expenditure method looks at final spending on the output. With the same period, scope and valuation, these are three views of the same production, not three totals to add together.
41	
42	An invented self-contained repair service illustrates the relationship. It sells N$1,000 of final repair services, uses no bought-in intermediate inputs in this simplified example, and generates wages N$700 plus profit N$300 with no other factor income. Final expenditure, value added and factor income each total N$1,000. Adding the three N$1,000 figures would count the same service three times.
43	
44	In real collection, records can be incomplete or timing and valuation can differ. A discrepancy does not mean the methods are intended to measure three independent economies. Consistency adjustments and statistical coverage matter. For a simple supplied case, first identify what the figure represents, then apply the relevant method using its boundary.
45	
46	The methods can be useful cross-checks. Output records can reveal a sector’s contribution; earnings records can describe income generated; spending records can show final demand composition. Their uses differ in emphasis even when they reconcile to the same overall activity. The following sections explain what each counts and the main repeated-counting error to avoid.
47	
48	Consistency also means recording the same production period. Payment for a service delivered earlier need not mean that service was produced again when the cash arrives. A production account and a cash-flow record answer different questions. The simplified examples assume their timing is aligned so the economic boundary can be seen clearly.
49	
50	### B-6145-7.3-006 Output method: count value added once
51	The output method sums value added across producers or the value of final output, using a consistent basis. Value added is output value minus the value of bought-in intermediate inputs. This prevents an input’s full value being counted at each stage as if it were new production each time. It is not the same as profit because labour and other factor rewards can be paid from value added.
52	
53	Use an invented chain with no other intermediate inputs. A grower sells produce for N$100 to a processor. The processor transforms it and sells to a household for N$250. The grower adds N$100 and the processor adds N$150, giving total value added N$250. Adding the two sales totals, N$350, would double count the produce’s N$100 value. The final purchase already embodies it.
54	
55	Now suppose the processor pays N$90 in wages from its N$150 value added and the remaining N$60 is profit under the simplified arrangement. Value added is still N$150, not only N$60. Subtracting wages to find profit serves a firm-accounting purpose; it is not the same operation as subtracting intermediate inputs to find value added.
56	
57	The method can reveal changes in sectors’ contributions. A larger value at current prices may reflect prices as well as quantities, so real comparisons need a consistent price basis. It is also important to cover relevant informal and non-market production as the chosen measure allows. Missing records can understate activity, but they should not be replaced with arbitrary invented additions in a calculation.
58	
59	### B-6145-7.3-007 Income method: count earned factor rewards
60	The income method sums factor incomes earned from current production on a consistent accounting basis. In the simple treatment these include wages, rent, interest and profit. The categories must not overlap and must relate to the period’s production. A loan received is a liability-financing transaction, not automatically additional earned income; a support transfer is a redistribution rather than a fresh factor reward.
61	
62	Using invented income categories of wages N$600, rent N$100, interest N$50 and profit N$250 gives N$1,000. If a worker saves N$100 of wages, the wage income is still earned. Saving changes how that income is used, not whether the original labour reward exists. Likewise, subsequently buying a household good is expenditure, not a second income-method entry for the buyer.
63	
64	Selling an existing financial asset shifts ownership and money between parties. The sale price itself is not proof of new output or new factor income. A separate service charge for arranging the sale can represent current service production, but that is a different item requiring its own facts. This boundary keeps large financial transfers from being mistaken for productive income.
65	
66	For a national rather than domestic income basis, the relevant resident and abroad adjustments must be consistent. Do not combine domestic wages with an unrelated national-profit figure without checking coverage. Data on recorded earnings can also miss activity where records are incomplete. The method is conceptually about income generated from production, not simply the sum of visible bank credits.
67	
68	### B-6145-7.3-008 Expenditure method: final spending on domestic output
69	The expenditure method sums final expenditure on domestically produced goods and services over the period. It includes final consumption and investment and the relevant government and external components under the stated convention. Exports are included because they buy domestic production; imports are excluded because that part of spending buys foreign production rather than current domestic output.
70	
71	An invented simple expenditure case supplies consumption N$500, investment N$200, government final purchases N$250, exports N$100 and imports N$50, all on a consistent basis. The total is N$500 + N$200 + N$250 + N$100 minus N$50, giving N$1,000. Imports are subtracted to remove foreign output included in the spending components, not because importing is inherently a loss in welfare.
72	
73	Do not add intermediate purchases again. In the produce example, household expenditure N$250 on the processed final product already includes the grower’s output. Adding the processor’s N$100 input purchase would repeat that value. Similarly, a government transfer is not itself a government purchase of a newly produced service; later spending by the recipient is classified where it occurs.
74	
75	Investment here concerns productive capital formation rather than merely depositing money in an account. Final use also does not mean useful for only a short time: equipment used to produce later output is investment. The distinction is its role in the production account, not whether an object is physically durable. Read each supplied transaction before assigning it to an expenditure component.
76	
77	### B-6145-7.3-009 Use the measures with their limits visible
78	National-income measures help describe the level and change of economic activity. Real comparisons across time can show whether production expands after allowing for prices. Sector figures can inform priorities by showing where value added is generated. A government can use these data to assess an employment or growth policy, while businesses may use them alongside other information about likely markets.
79	
80	Total and per-capita measures answer different questions. An invented real output N$1,000 million with population one million gives N$1,000 per person. Real output N$1,100 million with population 1.2 million gives about N$916.67 per person. The total grows but the average falls. Population can change through natural increase or migration; neither additional people alone nor a larger money total establishes improved real output per person.
81	
82	Even higher real output per person does not prove that all households are better off. Distribution can be unequal, environmental damage can impose costs, and leisure or service quality can change. Coverage of informal or unpaid activity may differ. Cross-country comparisons also need consistent definitions, prices and currency conversion. The measure is useful evidence of activity, not a complete welfare score.
83	
84	To explain a use, connect the data to a decision. A consistent real series can reveal a production slowdown and help target investigation. A sector contribution can guide further research into a bottleneck. The figures alone do not identify every cause or establish that one policy produced the change. Combine the measure with the relevant context, and use topic 8.2 for fuller living-standard assessment.
85	
86	An apparent improvement should therefore prompt a check of the denominator and price basis. More current-price output for a larger population can coexist with less real output per person. The three statements are compatible because they measure different aspects of the economy. Naming the precise measure makes the intended use and its limitation easier to explain.
87

# 7.3 Output

## Notes

### B-6145-7.3-001 Domestic, national and income describe different boundaries
National accounts measure production and the incomes and spending associated with it over a period. Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, concerns production within the territory. Gross National Product, or GNP, adjusts domestic product for net income earned from abroad by residents under the stated convention. National Income concerns income earned by a country’s factors of production. The names are related, but they do not permit every figure to be substituted for another without checking its definition.

Specify the period and basis before comparing. A monthly current-price total and an annual constant-price figure answer different questions. Domestic and national boundaries can differ where residents earn abroad or non-residents earn within the country. Gross and net measures also differ where capital-consumption allowance is deducted. These distinctions prevent a meaningful definition from becoming an unsupported numerical equality.

The simple invented cases below isolate one distinction at a time. They do not claim that current published national accounts contain no further adjustments. Where a question states a particular accounting convention, use it consistently and describe the measure actually obtained. Topic 5.3 measures an individual firm’s costs and revenue; the national account combines activity across producers while preventing repeated counting of the same production.

### B-6145-7.3-002 GDP: production inside the territory
Gross Domestic Product is the value of final goods and services produced within a country’s territory over a specified period, avoiding double counting. Final refers to output used for final consumption or investment rather than an input whose value is already included in another product. Services count alongside tangible goods. A year’s GDP is a flow of production, not the stock of wealth or cash balances at one date.

The domestic boundary follows location. If an invented non-resident-owned factory produces furniture inside Namibia, that production contributes to domestic output. Whether its owners later receive income abroad is relevant to a national-income adjustment, not a reason to erase the factory’s domestic production. Conversely, a resident’s production abroad does not become domestic output merely because the resident has a Namibian connection.

Current-price GDP values output at the prices of the period. It can rise because more is produced, prices rise or both. A real or constant-price comparison holds the price effect apart so changes in production can be examined. If the same quantities are valued 10% higher solely because prices rise, that is not evidence of a 10% expansion in real output.

GDP also differs from total sales of every producer added without adjustment. A material can be sold to a manufacturer and its value appear again in the final product. Counting both full values would repeat the intermediate component. The output method addresses that problem through value added, while the expenditure method focuses on final purchases.

### B-6145-7.3-003 GNP: adjust for net income from abroad
GNP adjusts domestic product for net factor income from abroad under the course’s stated convention. Add relevant income received from abroad by residents and subtract corresponding income paid to non-residents. Net means the difference between these opposing flows. It does not mean simply adding whichever foreign receipt is mentioned and ignoring payments outward.

Use invented annual figures in N$ million. Domestic product is 1,000, factor income received from abroad is 70 and factor income paid abroad is 90. Net income from abroad is 70 minus 90, or negative 20. GNP is therefore 980 on this specified basis. A negative net figure makes the national measure smaller than the domestic measure; it is not added as a positive 20.

The adjustment concerns factor income, not the trade balance. Exports and imports are purchases of output, while a factor-income flow is a reward from productive resources. An imported machine and a resident’s foreign interest receipt belong to different transactions. Their shared international character does not make them interchangeable in the adjustment.

Residence is also different from citizenship alone. The relevant national-accounting boundary concerns residents and their income under the stated convention. Do not decide inclusion merely from a passport description where the question supplies residence and production facts. The simple adjustment clarifies the domestic-national distinction without requiring an unsupported claim that every transfer from abroad is factor income.

### B-6145-7.3-004 National Income: earnings from production
National Income concerns the income earned by a country’s factors of production over a stated period. Wages reward labour; rent, interest and profit are other factor-income categories in the elementary treatment. The focus is earned income associated with production rather than every receipt of money. A transfer received without supplying current goods or services in exchange is not newly earned factor income.

Suppose an invented production example generates N$600 wages, N$100 rent, N$50 interest and N$250 profit, with all categories mutually exclusive and all relevant factor incomes included. Their sum is N$1,000. A separate N$80 support transfer to a household should not be added as new production income. It reallocates purchasing power rather than creating another N$80 of output.

The exact National Income measure depends on the accounting basis. A gross output value, a net income value and a value including product taxes need not be identical without adjustments. Gross means before capital-consumption allowance is deducted; net means after the relevant capital-consumption allowance adjustment. Use the convention supplied rather than inventing a bridge from one headline figure to another. The simple factor-income example sets aside such adjustments explicitly.

This discipline also helps prevent double counting profits. If wages have already been subtracted in arriving at the stated profit, adding wages and that profit counts different shares of value added. Adding sales receipts again would repeat the income generated by the same output. A household’s receipt and subsequent spending are connected stages, not two separate additions to National Income.

### B-6145-7.3-005 Three views of the same productive activity
The output method looks at what is produced or the value added by producers. The income method looks at the factor earnings generated. The expenditure method looks at final spending on the output. With the same period, scope and valuation, these are three views of the same production, not three totals to add together.

An invented self-contained repair service illustrates the relationship. It sells N$1,000 of final repair services, uses no bought-in intermediate inputs in this simplified example, and generates wages N$700 plus profit N$300 with no other factor income. Final expenditure, value added and factor income each total N$1,000. Adding the three N$1,000 figures would count the same service three times.

In real collection, records can be incomplete or timing and valuation can differ. A discrepancy does not mean the methods are intended to measure three independent economies. Consistency adjustments and statistical coverage matter. For a simple supplied case, first identify what the figure represents, then apply the relevant method using its boundary.

The methods can be useful cross-checks. Output records can reveal a sector’s contribution; earnings records can describe income generated; spending records can show final demand composition. Their uses differ in emphasis even when they reconcile to the same overall activity. The following sections explain what each counts and the main repeated-counting error to avoid.

Consistency also means recording the same production period. Payment for a service delivered earlier need not mean that service was produced again when the cash arrives. A production account and a cash-flow record answer different questions. The simplified examples assume their timing is aligned so the economic boundary can be seen clearly.

### B-6145-7.3-006 Output method: count value added once
The output method sums value added across producers or the value of final output, using a consistent basis. Value added is output value minus the value of bought-in intermediate inputs. This prevents an input’s full value being counted at each stage as if it were new production each time. It is not the same as profit because labour and other factor rewards can be paid from value added.

Use an invented chain with no other intermediate inputs. A grower sells produce for N$100 to a processor. The processor transforms it and sells to a household for N$250. The grower adds N$100 and the processor adds N$150, giving total value added N$250. Adding the two sales totals, N$350, would double count the produce’s N$100 value. The final purchase already embodies it.

Now suppose the processor pays N$90 in wages from its N$150 value added and the remaining N$60 is profit under the simplified arrangement. Value added is still N$150, not only N$60. Subtracting wages to find profit serves a firm-accounting purpose; it is not the same operation as subtracting intermediate inputs to find value added.

The method can reveal changes in sectors’ contributions. A larger value at current prices may reflect prices as well as quantities, so real comparisons need a consistent price basis. It is also important to cover relevant informal and non-market production as the chosen measure allows. Missing records can understate activity, but they should not be replaced with arbitrary invented additions in a calculation.

### B-6145-7.3-007 Income method: count earned factor rewards
The income method sums factor incomes earned from current production on a consistent accounting basis. In the simple treatment these include wages, rent, interest and profit. The categories must not overlap and must relate to the period’s production. A loan received is a liability-financing transaction, not automatically additional earned income; a support transfer is a redistribution rather than a fresh factor reward.

Using invented income categories of wages N$600, rent N$100, interest N$50 and profit N$250 gives N$1,000. If a worker saves N$100 of wages, the wage income is still earned. Saving changes how that income is used, not whether the original labour reward exists. Likewise, subsequently buying a household good is expenditure, not a second income-method entry for the buyer.

Selling an existing financial asset shifts ownership and money between parties. The sale price itself is not proof of new output or new factor income. A separate service charge for arranging the sale can represent current service production, but that is a different item requiring its own facts. This boundary keeps large financial transfers from being mistaken for productive income.

For a national rather than domestic income basis, the relevant resident and abroad adjustments must be consistent. Do not combine domestic wages with an unrelated national-profit figure without checking coverage. Data on recorded earnings can also miss activity where records are incomplete. The method is conceptually about income generated from production, not simply the sum of visible bank credits.

### B-6145-7.3-008 Expenditure method: final spending on domestic output
The expenditure method sums final expenditure on domestically produced goods and services over the period. It includes final consumption and investment and the relevant government and external components under the stated convention. Exports are included because they buy domestic production; imports are excluded because that part of spending buys foreign production rather than current domestic output.

An invented simple expenditure case supplies consumption N$500, investment N$200, government final purchases N$250, exports N$100 and imports N$50, all on a consistent basis. The total is N$500 + N$200 + N$250 + N$100 minus N$50, giving N$1,000. Imports are subtracted to remove foreign output included in the spending components, not because importing is inherently a loss in welfare.

Do not add intermediate purchases again. In the produce example, household expenditure N$250 on the processed final product already includes the grower’s output. Adding the processor’s N$100 input purchase would repeat that value. Similarly, a government transfer is not itself a government purchase of a newly produced service; later spending by the recipient is classified where it occurs.

Investment here concerns productive capital formation rather than merely depositing money in an account. Final use also does not mean useful for only a short time: equipment used to produce later output is investment. The distinction is its role in the production account, not whether an object is physically durable. Read each supplied transaction before assigning it to an expenditure component.

### B-6145-7.3-009 Use the measures with their limits visible
National-income measures help describe the level and change of economic activity. Real comparisons across time can show whether production expands after allowing for prices. Sector figures can inform priorities by showing where value added is generated. A government can use these data to assess an employment or growth policy, while businesses may use them alongside other information about likely markets.

Total and per-capita measures answer different questions. An invented real output N$1,000 million with population one million gives N$1,000 per person. Real output N$1,100 million with population 1.2 million gives about N$916.67 per person. The total grows but the average falls. Population can change through natural increase or migration; neither additional people alone nor a larger money total establishes improved real output per person.

Even higher real output per person does not prove that all households are better off. Distribution can be unequal, environmental damage can impose costs, and leisure or service quality can change. Coverage of informal or unpaid activity may differ. Cross-country comparisons also need consistent definitions, prices and currency conversion. The measure is useful evidence of activity, not a complete welfare score.

To explain a use, connect the data to a decision. A consistent real series can reveal a production slowdown and help target investigation. A sector contribution can guide further research into a bottleneck. The figures alone do not identify every cause or establish that one policy produced the change. Combine the measure with the relevant context, and use topic 8.2 for fuller living-standard assessment.

An apparent improvement should therefore prompt a check of the denominator and price basis. More current-price output for a larger population can coexist with less real output per person. The three statements are compatible because they measure different aspects of the economy. Naming the precise measure makes the intended use and its limitation easier to explain.

1	# 7.4 International trade
2	
3	## Notes
4	
5	### B-6145-7.4-001 Trade patterns and the external accounts
6	Exports sell output to other countries; imports buy output from them. A trade pattern describes the products, trading partners and values or quantities involved. A rise in export value can reflect higher prices, more units or both. It does not necessarily establish greater real production or improved profitability. Similarly, more imports can include productive equipment as well as consumer goods, so interpretation needs their composition.
7	
8	Use invented annual goods values in N$ million. Exports rise from 80 to 100 while imports rise from 90 to 120. Goods trade moves from a deficit of 10 to a deficit of 20 despite export growth. Comparing exports alone misses the faster import increase. The overall balance of payments also includes services, income, transfers and financial transactions, so this goods deficit is not a complete external account.
9	
10	An overseas investor acquiring a lasting ownership interest in an invented domestic workshop undertakes foreign direct investment. Its funding is a financial-account transaction, not simply a current-account export. The workshop’s later sale of goods abroad is a separate export transaction. Keeping flows distinct prevents external financing being mistaken for income from selling current output.
11	
12	Trade protection can influence patterns. A tariff taxes imports, while a quota limits their quantity under the stated rule. Both can reduce competitive pressure on some domestic producers but may raise buyer costs or affect input access. Topic 9.1 evaluates the conflicting interests and longer-term consequences; identify the mechanism here without assuming protection guarantees jobs or external stability.
13	
14	Changes in trading partners can also alter exposure. A producer selling most output to one foreign market may be vulnerable to that buyer’s demand conditions. Selling to several markets can spread some risk, although transport, standards and marketing costs may rise. Diversification is therefore a change in pattern with a possible benefit, not proof that every additional partner improves the external balance.
15	
16	The trade values must use the same currency and period. An export quantity can fall while its money value rises if prices increase enough. For example, 100 units at N$20 yield N$2,000, while 80 at N$30 yield N$2,400. Higher receipts here coexist with fewer units sold. The value table alone cannot establish the associated domestic employment or resource use.
17	
18	### B-6145-7.4-002 Exchange-rate causes and conditional effects
19	State the quotation first. If US$1 costs N$18 and later N$20, more Namibia dollars are needed for the same US dollar, so the Namibia dollar has depreciated against that third currency. Under the maintained one-to-one rand peg, this is not an independent N$/rand depreciation. Actual Namibia examples must preserve that distinction, as documented by the [Bank of Namibia](https://www.bon.com.na/Informations/FAQ/Roles-of-the-Bank.aspx).
20	
21	Currency demand can rise when foreign buyers purchase a country’s exports or investors seek its assets. Currency supply can rise when residents need foreign money for imports or overseas assets. In a hypothetical floating system, stronger demand for a currency with other conditions unchanged can raise its price; increased supply can lower it. Relative interest returns, expected inflation and confidence can influence these flows, but no factor determines the rate in isolation. The actual rand-peg framework constrains the Namibia case.
22	
23	A third-currency depreciation can make an unchanged foreign-currency import price more expensive domestically. An invented US$100 input costs N$1,800 at the first quotation and N$2,000 at the second. Exporters receiving dollars may receive more Namibia dollars for the same dollar sale, but imported inputs may also become dearer. A lower foreign-currency price can stimulate export quantities only if buyers respond and firms can supply.
24	
25	The trade balance is therefore not guaranteed to improve. Existing contracts may fix quantities or prices for a time, essential imports may be hard to reduce and export capacity may be limited. A firm with spare capacity and local inputs can respond differently from an importer with no substitute. Identify whose receipts and costs change, then assess the quantity response and period rather than drawing a conclusion from the currency direction alone.
26	
27	Appreciation against a third currency reverses the direct conversion effect: fewer domestic currency units buy the same foreign amount. This can ease an importer’s cost while reducing converted receipts from a fixed foreign-currency export sale. The competitive effect still depends on prices offered, inputs used and demand. A common currency movement can therefore benefit one business while creating a challenge for another, even within the same economy and maintained rand-peg framework.
28	
29	### B-6145-7.4-003 Calculate the sacrifice before recommending specialisation
30	Use two invented producers, A and B, each with its own fixed resource bundle for one period. A can make either 12 mats or 6 baskets; B can make either 4 mats or 4 baskets. Assume constant opportunity costs, comparable quality, divisible resource use and no transport costs. A produces more of either good from its bundle, so it has absolute advantage in both. That does not prevent mutually useful specialisation.
31	
32	For A, one mat sacrifices 6/12, or half a basket. For B, one mat sacrifices 4/4, or one basket. A has comparative advantage in mats because its sacrifice is lower. Reverse the ratios for baskets: A sacrifices 2 mats per basket; B sacrifices 1. B has comparative advantage in baskets despite lower absolute output. The relevant comparison changes with the concept being tested.
33	
34	At full specialisation, A makes 12 mats and B 4 baskets. Suppose they exchange 3 mats for 2 baskets, equivalent to 1.5 mats per basket. A obtains each imported basket for fewer mats than the 2 it would sacrifice producing it. B receives more mats per basket than the 1 it could make by sacrificing a basket itself. Both gain access to more favourable exchange than their own opportunity costs.
35	
36	After that trade A has 9 mats and 2 baskets; B has 3 mats and 2 baskets. These combinations lie beyond what each could produce alone under its schedule. This is not a claim that full specialisation raises every good’s aggregate output from any chosen starting allocation. The gain is demonstrated through feasible consumption and the trade terms. Transport costs, imperfect mobility, different quality or changing opportunity costs can reduce the simple model’s benefit.
37	
38	Check the individual opportunity explicitly. To produce 2 baskets alone, A would sacrifice 4 mats and have only 8 mats left; trade leaves it 9 mats with the same 2 baskets. B producing 3 mats alone would sacrifice 3 baskets and have only 1 basket left; trade leaves it 2 baskets with those 3 mats. Each obtains a combination unavailable from its own resources alone. This comparison supplies evidence of a potential gain without assuming both would prefer an identical consumption mix.
39	
40	### B-6145-7.4-004 Absolute advantage: compare resource productivity
41	Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources or requiring fewer resources for the same output. In the invented maximum-output schedule, A’s 12 mats exceed B’s 4 and A’s 6 baskets exceed B’s 4. The comparison uses matched resource bundles and periods. Comparing different-sized countries’ raw totals without considering resources would not establish productive efficiency in this sense.
42	
43	The word absolute concerns the output or resource requirement, not the sacrifice of the alternative good. It answers a useful question but cannot replace the comparative calculation. A can be absolutely better in both activities while B sacrifices less of one good to make the other. Choosing trade specialisation from the bigger output number alone would miss that relative difference.
44	
45	### B-6145-7.4-005 Comparative advantage: compare opportunity costs
46	Comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost. Express the sacrifice in units of the other good, not as a bare ratio. In the invented schedule, A’s cost of one mat is half a basket, while B’s is one basket. For one basket the costs are 2 mats and 1 mat respectively, so B has the basket advantage. Label both the good being produced and the alternative sacrificed to avoid reversing the result.
47	
48	Trade terms need to fall between the relevant opportunity costs for both to gain in this simple case. At 1.5 mats per basket, A pays less than its own 2 and B receives more than its own 1. Terms at a boundary leave one party with no strict improvement from that unit exchange; terms outside can disadvantage one side. Comparative advantage supports a conditional opportunity for trade, not an obligation to accept any offered price.
49
